units.translation: ἐξελοῦσ᾽ [having taken out] M. ἐκζέουσ᾽ [boiling over] Musgravius, which the scholiast seems to have read, who explains it by ἀναπτερώσασα [having stirred up]. On the transitive use of the verb see Hermann's note.
For the curses of Oedipus boiled over.
Do not, boiling over like the heart of cocks, establish Ares among my citizens.
Be at ease, and do not be overly afraid.
After Aeschylus no one is found to have used this verb except Tzetzes, for whose examples see Thes. vol. 3 p. 416.
Do not utterly destroy my city from its roots.
And the liver, blackened with gore, will be devoured.
They leapt out of the ships.
He cleanses this land of man-destroying monsters.
Joy creeps over me, calling forth a tear.
Uncover everything and tell us the story.

where the Ionic form is to be noted.
This city of Susa he emptied when it fell.
The city cries out as it is being emptied.
The Asian land groans as it is being emptied.
Hesychius: ἐξεκήρανεν [he destroyed utterly] — ἐξέφθειρε [he corrupted], just as the same author explains κηραίνει [he harms] among other things by φθείρει [he destroys].
They destroyed the might of the terrible serpent.
Either someone stole it or sought it.
the best men, chosen from the city.

the chosen multitude of the army.

about the Sphinx fixed on the shield of Parthenopaeus

Eustath. p. 1160, 40: ἴσως δὲ καὶ μηχανῇ τινι ἐκινοῦντο [perhaps they were moved by some device] (the figures on the shield) ἔκκρουστα ὄντα καὶ οὐ διόλου προσηλωμένα τῷ σάκει [being movable and not nailed all the way through to the shield], καὶ οὕτως ἐφάνταζον τοῖς ὁρῶσι τὸ αὐτοκίνητον [and thus they presented to the viewers the appearance of self-motion], ὁποῖον δή τι πλάττει καὶ Αἰσχύλος ἐν τοῖς Ἑπτὰ ἐπὶ Θήβαις [such as Aeschylus also represents in the Seven against Thebes].
For the disgrace of the city, on a bronze-wrought shield — a Sphinx, raw-flesh-eating, fitted on, he moved with bolts, a shining, movable body.

in what way he will be rolled out of this fortune.

before he leaps into my house and drives out the foals from their seats with the spear.
